_: The reserved-word sets of the four SDK target languages, committed as DATA so the collision figure is re-derivable without trusting a predicate somebody typed into a script. Every set carries the normative source it was copied from and the count that source states. `survey/keyword_collisions.py` reads this file and cross-checks the two sets a running interpreter can confirm (`python.hard_keywords` against `keyword.kwlist`, `python.soft_keywords` against `keyword.softkwlist`), so a drift between this file and CPython is a refusal rather than a wrong number.

hard_keywords.source: The Python Language Reference 3.12 section 2.3.1 'Keywords' (https://docs.python.org/3.12/reference/lexical_analysis.html#keywords), which is what CPython's `Lib/keyword.py` is generated from (`Grammar/python.gram`). Re-derivable: `python3.12 -c 'import keyword; print(keyword.kwlist)'`.

soft_keywords.source: The Python Language Reference 3.12 section 2.3.2 'Soft Keywords' (https://docs.python.org/3.12/reference/lexical_analysis.html#soft-keywords). Re-derivable: `python3.12 -c 'import keyword; print(keyword.softkwlist)'`.
soft_keywords.why_it_is_a_softer_class: A soft keyword IS a valid identifier -- `match = 1`, `type = 4`, `_ = 5` all bind -- so it needs no mangling anywhere. Measured on CPython 3.12.13: all four assign.

enum_protocol.source: `enum` -- Support for enumerations, Python 3.12 (https://docs.python.org/3.12/library/enum.html); CPython `Lib/enum.py`, where `Enum.name` and `Enum.value` are declared as `types.DynamicClassAttribute`.
enum_protocol.why_it_is_a_softer_class: `DynamicClassAttribute` exists PRECISELY so that a member may be called `name` or `value`: the descriptor raises on class access, `EnumType.__getattr__` then resolves the name out of `_member_map_`, and the member comes back. Measured on CPython 3.12.13: `class K(StrEnum): name = 'name'` gives `K.name -> <K.name: 'name'>`, `K['name']` the same object, and `K('name') is K.name`. So these two cost a mangling only where a SECOND attribute per member is also wanted -- see `alias_cost` in the instrument.

reserved_words.source: ECMA-262 section 12.7.2 'Keywords and Reserved Words', the `ReservedWord` production (https://tc39.es/ecma262/#sec-keywords-and-reserved-words).

strict_mode_reserved_words.source: ECMA-262 section 12.7.2, the words that 'cannot be used as identifiers in strict mode code' (https://tc39.es/ecma262/#sec-keywords-and-reserved-words); the early errors are section 13.1.1.

type_position_keywords.source: Not an ECMA-262 set: these are TypeScript's own predeclared TYPE names. Measured against `tsc 5.9.3 --strict --target es2022 --noEmit`, which is how the list was confirmed rather than read off a spec that does not state it (the normative TypeScript grammar is `src/compiler/types.ts`, and the last published language specification -- v1.8 section 2.2.3 -- predates most of these).
type_position_keywords.where_it_bites: `export type any = string` is an error; `export const any = 1` is NOT. So these collide only in a TYPE-ALIAS-NAME position and nowhere else.

object_prototype.source: ECMA-262 section 20.1.3, the properties of `Object.prototype` (https://tc39.es/ecma262/#sec-properties-of-the-object-prototype-object), plus the `__proto__` accessor of section B.2.2.1. A TypeScript `enum` compiles to a plain object, so a member spelled like one of these shadows an inherited property of it.
object_prototype.why_it_is_a_softer_class: Measured: `tsc 5.9.3 --strict` accepts `enum E { constructor = "constructor" }`. A member shadowing `Object.prototype` is legal and only matters to code that reflects over the enum object. This is TypeScript's nearest analogue of Python's `Enum.name`/`Enum.value` and of Java's `Enum.name()`, and it is listed so the protocol-collision count can be stated for all four targets rather than for two.

enum_member_names_may_be_reserved_words.source: Measured, not asserted. `tsc 5.9.3 --strict --target es2022 --noEmit` accepts `export enum E { class = "class", if = "if", new = "new", pass = "pass", global = "global", name = "name", value = "value", await = "await", let = "let", enum = "enum", true = "true", null = "null", constructor = "constructor", function = "function", var = "var", typeof = "typeof", in = "in", delete = "delete" }` with exit status 0, and accepts a quoted member name `enum E2 { "media-buy" = "media-buy" }` as well.
enum_member_names_may_be_reserved_words.why: An `EnumMember`'s name is a `PropertyName`, which admits any `IdentifierName` -- and `IdentifierName`, unlike `Identifier`, includes every reserved word. This is the same rule that makes `{ class: 1 }` a legal object literal.

keywords.source: The Go Programming Language Specification, 'Keywords' (https://go.dev/ref/spec#Keywords), which states 'The following keywords are reserved and may not be used as identifiers' and lists 25.

predeclared_identifiers.source: The Go Programming Language Specification, 'Predeclared identifiers' (https://go.dev/ref/spec#Predeclared_identifiers): 22 types, 3 constants, the zero value `nil`, and 18 functions. Cross-checked against the toolchain's own `$(go env GOROOT)/src/builtin/builtin.go` at go1.26.8, which declares exactly these 44 names plus six documentation placeholders (`Type`, `Type1`, `IntegerType`, `FloatType`, `ComplexType`, `TypeOrExpr`) that are not predeclared identifiers and are excluded.
predeclared_identifiers.why_it_is_still_listed: A predeclared identifier is in the universe block, so a declaration in any inner scope shadows it legally. It is listed because the shadow is silent: a package-level `const Error = "error"` leaves `error` usable, but a local `len := 3` makes `len(x)` a compile error later in the same function, and a reader of the generated file cannot see which it is.

exported_identifiers_are_capitalised.source: The Go Programming Language Specification, 'Exported identifiers' (https://go.dev/ref/spec#Exported_identifiers): an identifier is exported if 'the first character of the identifier's name is a Unicode upper case letter'.
exported_identifiers_are_capitalised.why_it_matters_here: Every Go keyword and every predeclared identifier is entirely lower-case, so capitalising the first rune escapes all 69 of them outright. What capitalisation does NOT escape -- and what no other target language's convention escapes either -- is two values in one enum that differ only by case or by a separator. That is the Go-specific collision this instrument measures.

keywords.source: The Java Language Specification, Java SE 21, section 3.9 'Keywords' (https://docs.oracle.com/javase/specs/jls/se21/html/jls-3.html#jls-3.9): 50 character sequences 'formed from ASCII letters', plus the underscore, 'reserved ... and cannot be used as identifiers'.

literals.source: The Java Language Specification, Java SE 21, sections 3.10.3 (`true`, `false`) and 3.10.8 (`null`). They are not keywords but they may not be used as identifiers either.

contextual_keywords.source: The Java Language Specification, Java SE 21, section 3.9: 'a contextual keyword ... is a keyword only where it appears in a specific context, and is otherwise an ordinary identifier'.
contextual_keywords.why_it_is_a_softer_class: A contextual keyword is a legal identifier everywhere else, so an enum constant may be called `record` or `var` or `yield`. Listed so that a hit on one is reported as the soft class it is instead of being silently counted with the 51.

enum_members.source: `java.lang.Enum`, Java SE 21 API (https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/api/java.base/java/lang/Enum.html), plus the two static methods the compiler synthesises onto every enum class (JLS 21 section 8.9.3: `values()` and `valueOf(String)`).
enum_members.why_it_is_a_softer_class: Java puts fields and methods in SEPARATE namespaces (JLS 21 section 6.5.6 resolves an `ExpressionName` against fields and section 15.12 resolves a `MethodName` against methods), and an enum constant is a static FIELD. So `enum E { name }` declares `E.name` beside the inherited `name()` and both resolve: a constant spelled like one of these is a readability hazard, not a compile error. `Enum.name` itself is a PRIVATE field of `Enum`, and a private field is not inherited, so it is not shadowed either.

constants_are_upper_snake_by_convention.source: The Java Language Specification, Java SE 21, section 6.1 'Declarations': 'The names of constants in interface types should be, and `final` variables of class types may conventionally be, a sequence of one or more words, acronyms, or abbreviations, all uppercase, with components separated by underscore characters.' Section 8.9.1's own examples (`SUNDAY`, `MONDAY`, ... ; `MERCURY`, `VENUS`) are enum constants written that way.
constants_are_upper_snake_by_convention.why_it_matters_here: Every one of the 51 keywords and all three literals are entirely lower-case, and `String.toUpperCase` moves every one of them, so UPPER_SNAKE escapes the whole hard class -- and it escapes the six `Enum` member names too. What it does NOT escape is the case/separator fold, which it makes STRICTLY WORSE than Go's: `clickTag` and `clickTAG` both become `CLICK_TAG` under a camel-aware split and `CLICKTAG` under a naive one.
